𝗜𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗮 “𝗻𝗼.”
But it came with clarity I didn’t have before.

Recently, I went through the Amazon SDE II (L5) interview process in London.
It ended in a rejection.
But the experience? It taught me more than any successful offer ever did.

Here’s what I learned — not just about interviews, but about how we grow as engineers.

🔹 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.
I could explain how LRU cache works in O(1). But I couldn’t code it well under pressure.
Understanding isn’t the bottleneck — fluency is.
So practice writing clean, bug-free code for hard problems, under time constraints.

🔹 𝗕𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗻’𝘁 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲.
Amazon heavily evaluates you on their Leadership Principles.
I had examples — but not all were crisp or layered enough.
Good stories have context, action, and measurable impact. Make them count.

🔹 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗸𝗶𝘁.
In my system design round, I clearly shared where my knowledge stopped — and it worked in my favor.
If you don't know something, say so.
Then walk through how you'd approach solving it. That's what they care about.

🔹 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗮𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.
After every round, I reflected honestly — did I explain well? Did I rush? Did I listen?
It helped me stay grounded and improve in real-time, not just after the process ended.

𝗧𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗙𝗔𝗔𝗡𝗚-𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀:
✅ Master the fundamentals
✅ Practice structured communication
✅ Treat behavioral prep as first-class
✅ Code under pressure — like the real thing
✅ Reflect, improve, repeat

I didn’t get the offer.
But I got better.

That’s enough for now.

# How I Got My Amazon Offer…

5 min read

Apr 26, 2026

--

Share

## How It Started

I applied through Amazon’s careers portal like any normal application — no referral, no shortcut.

I came across the opportunity while regularly checking job openings and staying active on LinkedIn, where I usually track roles from companies I’m interested in.

Back in June–July 2025, I took the first step in my Amazon interview journey — the Online Assessment (OA).

## Round 0: Online Assessment (OA)

The Online Assessment was divided into two parts:

### 1. DSA Round (1 hour)

- 2 coding questions
- Difficulty: Easy to Medium
- Platform: HackerRank

Nothing out of the ordinary here.

### 2. Leadership Principles Round (1 hour)

This is where things get interesting.

- Scenario-based questions
- You’re given situations and asked how you’d respond
- Every question maps to Amazon’s Leadership Principles

It’s not about “right answers.”It’s about consistency in your thinking.

### The Long Wait… and the Call

After the OA, there was silence for months.

Then in January 2026, I got the onsite call.

That’s when the real game started.

## Round 1: DSA + Problem Solving Mindset

This round was conducted at the Amazon office.

### Interview Setup

- 2 interviewers:
- Engineering Manager (~10 years experience)
- Tech Lead (~7 years experience)
- Format: Whiteboard coding (no laptop)

### The Question

Sliding Window Maximum

This is a classic problem — but the way you approach it matters more than just solving it.

Instead of jumping straight to the optimal solution, I:

1. Started with brute force
2. Explained why it’s inefficient
3. Gradually moved toward optimization

This is something many candidates skip — but interviewers care a lot about your thinking process.

### Discussion Flow

- Explained multiple approaches
- Compared trade-offs
- Finally implemented the optimized solution on the whiteboard

### Then came follow-ups:

- Time Complexity?
- Space Complexity?
- Can it be optimized further?
- What about concurrency?

That last one stood out — they were testing if I can think beyond DSA.

### Behavioral + Experience

Toward the end:

- Questions from my past projects
- A short Leadership Principles discussion (~10 mins)
- “Why are you a good fit for this role?”

### Verdict

This round went well because:

- I communicated clearly
- Didn’t rush
- Showed structured thinking

## Round 2: System Design + Deep Dive Thinking

This was a 1.5-hour round with a Senior Engineering Manager (23 years experience).

### Start: Resume Deep Dive

Before any problem:

- “Why did you build this?”
- “How did you design it?”
- “What challenges did you face?”

This wasn’t surface-level — he went deep.

### The Problem

Design a system:

A folder/file structure where:

- Folders can contain folders (nested deeply)
- Files exist at any level
- You must support searching files using regex

### What Made This Round Unique

I initially started with High-Level Design (HLD).

But he stopped me and said:

“Write code. Pseudocode. Right now.

This completely shifted the direction.

## What I Built

On pen and paper:

- Folder structure representation
- Recursive traversal
- Search logic
- Regex matching
- Multiple helper functions

### Then It Got Harder

He kept extending the problem:

### 1. Advanced Search

- Search by file name
- Search by file size

### 2. Performance Constraints

“What if there are 100 levels of nesting?

My answer:

- Introduced caching
- Avoid repeated traversal

### 3. Controlled Depth Search

“Don’t go beyond 5 levels”

I implemented:

- Recursion with depth control
- Early stopping condition

### Leadership Round (End)

~15 minutes of scenario-based questions again.

### Key Learning from Round 2

This wasn’t just system design.

It was:

- Coding
- Scalability thinking
- Real-world constraints
- Depth over breadth

## Round 3: When Things Started Going Wrong

This round lasted around 1.5 hours and was taken by a Senior Manager (~16 years experience).

### The Start — Not Smooth

- We began with introductions
- Quickly moved into a discussion around AI in software development

And this is where things got… uncomfortable.

### The Disagreement

The interviewer strongly believed:

AI can be used in ~90% of development work.

I didn’t fully agree.

My stance was:

AI is helpful for writing code, but engineers must fully understand everything before it goes to production — because ownership and responsibility still lie with us.

This created a visible disagreement.

And from that moment, I could feel:

- He wasn’t aligned with my thinking
- The tone of the interview shifted

### Leadership Principles (20 mins)

We spent a good amount of time here.

But honestly:

- He still didn’t seem convinced
- The conversation felt slightly off-track

### The DSA Question

Rearrange a string such that no two adjacent characters are the same

### What Went Wrong

- I started explaining my approach
- Defined constraints
- Walked through logic

But he wasn’t satisfied.

The discussion kept drifting.

At this point, many candidates panic.

### The Turning Point

Instead of pushing harder, I did something different.

I asked:

“Can you share your approach?”

He explained his solution with logic and corner cases.

And then — I analyzed his approach live and pointed out edge cases where it could fail.

### Why This Worked

This changed everything.

- The conversation became collaborative
- It showed I can think critically, not just follow
- It demonstrated confidence without arrogance

After that:

- I re-explained my approach
- Covered Time & Space Complexity
- Addressed edge cases clearly

And now — he was aligned.

### Momentum Shift

This entire turnaround happened in ~45 minutes.

Then he said:

“You solved this early… should we try another one?”

That’s when I knew things had flipped.

### Next Problem (Tree + Graph Twist)

### Problem Setup

- Company hierarchy
- Each employee has:
- `id`
- `manager`
- CEO has no manager

### Task

Find the common manager of two employees.

### My Approach

First:

- Solved it like Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in a tree

Then he extended:

“Now assume each employee also has a list of subordinates — like a graph.”

### Second Extension

- Converted thinking to graph traversal
- Handled bidirectional relationships
- Solved again with adjusted logic

### End of Round 3

By the end:

- The interviewer was satisfied
- The energy had completely changed

Within 5 minutes, I was moved to the next round.

## Round 4: The Deepest Dive

This round started almost immediately.

### Interviewer

- From Amazon Prime Video (London)
- ~15 years experience

### A New Challenge — Communication

There was a clear accent gap.

- There was a clear accent gap. I could understand him well despite the differences between Indian and UK English accents.
- He struggled a bit with my pace.

So I adapted:

- Spoke slower
- Structured answers clearly

## This Round Was Different

No DSA.

This was:

- Projects + Leadership Principles

## How Deep He Went

If your project was a person…

He didn’t stop at the face.

He went into:

“How does the hair work?”

That level of depth.

### What He Focused On

- Why did you build this?
- How exactly does it work?
- What decisions did you make?
- What trade-offs did you consider?

This wasn’t about buzzwords.

It was about:

Ownership and clarity

### End of Round

~30–40 minutes in:

- He was satisfied
- The tone was positive

### The Result

After one week, I got the call: You are selected.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

## What Actually Made the Difference

Looking back, it wasn’t just DSA or System Design.

## 1. Communication > Perfection

- Explaining clearly mattered more than writing perfect code

## 2. Recovery Matters More Than Performance

- Round 3 almost went wrong
- Recovery changed everything

## 3. Depth Over Surface Knowledge

- Especially in system design and project rounds

## 4. Ownership Mindset

- Amazon really tests this everywhere

## Final Thought

Most people think interviews are about getting everything right.

They’re not.

They’re about:

How you think when things go wrong.

🎯 Interview Experience

It’s been two months since I joined Amazon London, and I've been getting a
lot of questions from friends and peers about the interview process and how I
prepared for it. So, I thought I’d share a breakdown of the 3-round interview
experience I went through. It wasn’t just about coding — it really tested how I
think, collaborate, and reflect on past experiences.

I wanted to just post the actual questions I was asked — because sometimes, just knowing what to expect can help a lot while preparing.

🔹 Round 1 – Situational + Coding
1.   Tell me about a time when you worked out of your comfort zone or picked up work you usually don’t do.
2.   When were you not able to fulfil a commitment?
3.   Tell me about a time when the deadline was tight — what did you do to manage it?

Coding:
File system-based question

The question included searching through a directory to find a file with certain
extension i.e..xml,.exe also having specific file size — moderate difficulty. Having familiarity with system libraries helped a lot here. Gave a mix of working code and pseudocode.

🔹 Round 2 – Projects, Teamwork & Coding
1.   Which project do you love the most and why?
2.   When was another time you couldn't complete a commitment (other than the previous one)?
3.   Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate — how did you resolve it?
4.   How many hackathons did you participate in after your first one, and what did you learn from them?

Coding:
Word Search (LeetCode) — deep dive into time complexity and optimization
techniques.

🔹 Round 3 – Deep Dives + OOP Design
1.   Tell me about a time when you had to get to the root cause of a problem.
2.   Tell me about a time when you had to go deep into a topic to accomplish something.

Coding:
A class-based design problem
The Question was to implement a package sorting where you have package of sizes small, medium and large and you have been given lockers as well in which you can put them. Along with this needed to write delivery logic.
Walked through data structures and design choices. Along with this I was asked
about the time complexity of every data structure as well.

✅ Some Final Tips (from my own prep +
experience):
1.  Have real stories ready — your college projects, group work, side gigs, even failed attempts can become strong answers if you reflect on them well.
2.  Don’t just prepare to code — prepare to explain your thinking. That’s what most interviewers are really looking for.
3.  Time complexity matters — especially in later rounds. Be ready to break it down.

And lastly, treat the interview like a conversation, not a quiz. It helps ease the
pressure and makes your personality come through. If you're prepping for interviews — feel free to reach out, or drop a comment.
Happy to help however I can! 😊

**Kaustav Saha**: SDE II at Amazon for 3 years 10 months with 14 years 4 months of total professional experience. Previous roles include Full Stack Engineer at Vimeo, Software Designer at Micro Focus, and Tech Lead at Honeywell. Based in London Area, United Kingdom [GB].

---

Every system design round I bombed had the same pattern.

The interviewer said "design a URL shortener" or "design Twitter"

And I immediately started drawing boxes and arrows.

Databases. Servers. Caches. Load balancers.

I thought that's what they wanted to see.

It wasn't the case.

What they actually want to see is how you think.

The boxes come later. First, you need to ask questions.

Because "design Twitter" is not a real problem.

"Design a feed that 300 million people can read, where posts show up within 10 seconds, and the system keeps running even if one server crashes"

Now, that's a real problem.

Before you draw anything, ask:

→ How many people will use this?
→ Do they mostly read or mostly write?
→ What happens if part of the system goes down?
→ What does "this is broken" look like for a user?

Different answers = completely different designs.

The candidates who stand out aren't the ones with the most technical knowledge.

They're the ones who ask the best questions.

Next time you practice, spend the first 5 minutes just talking, no drawing.

You'll be surprised how much better your design gets.

# My Experience Interviewing for an Amazon Android Software Engineer Role in London

3 min read

Jan 28, 2025

--

Share

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Amazon Interview

Today, I had the exciting opportunity to interview for an Android Software Engineer position at Amazon in London. It was a challenging yet insightful experience, and I thought I’d share the details of how the day unfolded.

The Technical AssessmentThe interview kicked off with two HackerRank coding challenges. The first was a medium-level question, which focused on optimizing an algorithm to handle a specific problem. It was a great test of my ability to work with data structures and optimize the solution for efficiency. I felt confident while working through it, carefully analyzing edge cases and making sure my solution was optimal within the given constraints.

The second question was more challenging — labeled “hard” on HackerRank. This problem required me to think deeply and take a more systematic approach to reach a solution. I spent a lot of time breaking it down into smaller, manageable steps, but even after my best efforts, I couldn’t get the final solution to work as I hoped. Nevertheless, I ensured to keep the interviewer informed about my thought process, explaining each step of my approach. The feedback from the interviewer was constructive, and they appreciated how I tried to optimize the solution, even if it wasn’t fully complete.

They allotted a total of 1 hour and 30 minutes for these two coding challenges, and the time pressure was real. I had to manage both the complexity of the questions and my time wisely. The experience pushed me to sharpen my problem-solving skills and focus on communication.

Cultural Fit and Behavioral QuestionsAfter the coding portion, the interview shifted to cultural fit questions. Amazon is famous for its leadership principles, so I was asked several questions revolving around these principles, designed to understand how I align with Amazon’s culture.

Some of the questions I was asked were:

- “Tell me about a time when you took ownership of a project and delivered results.”
- “Describe a situation where you had to disagree with your team members. How did you handle it?”
- “How do you make data-driven decisions when you’re faced with ambiguity?”

These types of questions required me to pull from my previous work experiences and demonstrate how I reflect Amazon’s values. It wasn’t just about technical ability but also about how I approach challenges and work within teams. I made sure to explain the situations clearly and show how I’ve continuously learned and grown from past experiences.

Situation-Based Work QuestionsThe final section of the interview involved more situation-based questions, where I was asked to describe specific work-related challenges I’ve encountered and how I navigated them. One particular question that stood out was about a time when I had to manage tight deadlines while maintaining quality in my work. I talked about a project where I had to balance customer needs with technical limitations, all while leading a small team. The interviewer was particularly interested in my decision-making process and how I handled high-pressure situations.

Another question asked how I handle conflict within teams. I gave an example of a time when there was a disagreement about project direction, and I had to mediate between conflicting opinions to find a solution that benefited the project. This was an opportunity to show not just technical skill but also emotional intelligence and leadership under pressure.

ConclusionLooking back at the interview, I feel both challenged and proud. The technical portion of the interview tested my coding and problem-solving skills, pushing me to think critically under time constraints. While I didn’t manage to complete the second HackerRank question, I still felt positive about how I communicated my approach.

The cultural fit and behavioral questions provided me with a chance to demonstrate how I align with Amazon’s values and how I navigate real-world work situations. Overall, the interview was a great opportunity to reflect on my growth, my technical capabilities, and my ability to contribute to a team in a leadership role.

I’m eagerly awaiting the next steps and looking forward to future challenges, knowing that this experience has already made me better at handling similar situations in the future.

What My Amazon UK (London) SDE Online Assessment Looked Like 🇬🇧💻

I recently completed the Amazon UK (London) Software Development Engineer Online Assessment, and I wanted to share what the assessment looked like from my experience.
The assessment had 4 main sections:

🔹 1. Coding Challenge – 100 minutes
The coding section had two different challenges:
• Coding Question 1:
A Dynamic Programming problem on strings, with around 45 minutes to solve it.

• Coding Question 2:
A Java + Spring Boot + React repository-based challenge.
The second challenge was different from a traditional DSA question. I had to work with an existing movie website codebase and identify and fix a bug in the search feature.
This required understanding the existing code, tracing the search functionality, identifying the issue, making the required changes, and testing the solution.

🔹 2. Work Simulation – 45 minutes
This section focused on realistic software engineering situations and decision-making, including how you would handle different workplace scenarios.

🔹 3. Work Style Surveys – 15 minutes
Two surveys focused on work style, engineering preferences, and how you approach different situations at work.
Overall, the assessment tested much more than just DSA.

One thing I found particularly interesting was the repository-based challenge, because it felt closer to working on a real software project than solving a standalone coding problem.
Sharing this experience for anyone preparing for an Amazon SDE Online Assessment.
